---
title: "Masks: Choosing What Counts"
---

A filter decides which observations can contribute. A weight decides how strongly they contribute.

Both can be represented by a signal on the same addresses as the data.

## 🔰 A binary mask selects addresses {#sec-sample-masks-a-binary-mask-selects-addresses}

For $S=(1,2,2,5)$, let

$$
W=(0,1,0,1).
$$

The selected record contains the values at addresses two and four:

$$
S|_W=(2,5).
$$

Its mean is $3.5$.

Multiplying pointwise instead gives

$$
W\odot S=(0,2,0,5).
$$

This has the original four addresses. Its mean is $1.75$ because the two inserted zeros still count as values.

Selection and zeroing are distinct operations. Their totals agree, but their observation counts differ.

## 🏵 Let the denominator follow the selection {#sec-sample-masks-let-the-denominator-follow-the-selection}

For nonnegative weights with positive total, define

$$
M_W(S)
=
\frac{\sum_tW[t]S[t]}
     {\sum_tW[t]}.
$$

When the weights are zero or one, the denominator counts the selected observations. Our example gives $(2+5)/2=3.5$.

If the mask selects nothing, the denominator is zero. There is no selected mean to report.

A missing value also needs a missing-data rule. In numerical software, multiplying a missing-value marker by zero does not necessarily remove it. Form the valid selected observations before reducing them.

## ⚙️ Weights can carry different meanings {#sec-sample-masks-weights-can-carry-different-meanings}

Consider

$$
W=(1,1,1,2).
$$

The weighted mean of the record is

$$
\frac{1+2+2+2(5)}{1+1+1+2}=3.
$$

As frequency weights, this is the mean of an expanded record containing two copies of the final value.

The same arithmetic can be used with reliability weights or sampling weights. Those meanings need different justifications and may imply different uncertainty calculations.

The formula describes how values are combined. It does not decide why one observation deserves more influence.

## 💡 A logical question can produce a mask {#sec-sample-masks-a-logical-question-can-produce-a-mask}

Let the predicate be “value greater than one.” Evaluating it at every observation produces

$$
W[t]=\mathbf1_{\{S[t]>1\}}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
W=(0,1,1,1).
$$

This selects $(2,2,5)$.

A fuzzy membership rule could instead supply a grade at each address. Using those grades as averaging weights would be a further, explicit operation; the weighted mean would not turn membership into event probability.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-sample-mask-rule
%%| fig-cap: "The data supplies values; a condition supplies aligned weights. The reduction needs both weighted contributions and their denominator."
flowchart TD
    S["Observed signal"] --> C["Evaluate condition"]
    C --> W["Aligned mask or weights"]
    S --> N["Weighted contributions"]
    W --> N
    W --> D["Weight total"]
    N --> M["Weighted mean"]
    D --> M
```

## ☯ A mask on possibilities leads to conditioning {#sec-sample-masks-a-mask-on-possibilities-leads-to-conditioning}

We can also select within a generator's possible outcomes. Retain the possibilities compatible with an event, then renormalize their remaining probability mass.

The operation resembles selection in a record, but the domain has changed: possibilities instead of observed addresses.

[Conditioning](conditioning.qmd) develops that construction. Keeping the two domains separate lets the same idea travel without changing its meaning invisibly.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try the idea {#sec-sample-masks-try-the-idea}

For $S=(1,2,2,5)$, select values greater than one. What are the selected mean and the mean of the zeroed four-address signal?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Work it through {#sec-sample-masks-work-it-through}

The selected record is $(2,2,5)$, with mean $9/3=3$. The zeroed signal is $(0,2,2,5)$, with mean $9/4=2.25$. Their equal total hides a different denominator.
:::
